script.opening: “Every time we cut the steroids, the stiffness comes straight back. I can barely get out of bed. I want to go back to 15 milligrams, that worked, and just stay on it.”

facts.text: Twice now: each time the dose went below 7.5 mg, the aching and stiffness in her shoulders, upper arms, hips and thighs returned within two weeks, with morning stiffness over an hour. Like the original illness.

facts.topic: Only if asked exactly how she is taking her tablets
facts.text: Ten days ago she went back up to 15 mg herself using an old box from the start of treatment. Feels much better already. Stopped the weekly alendronate three months ago because of heartburn; did not tell anyone. Still taking lansoprazole.
No new headache, no scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, no jaw pain on chewing, no visual blurring, double vision or loss. No fever, sweats or weight loss.

No swollen small joints in her hands or feet. No back pain at night. No cough. Weight up 6 kg since starting steroids. Bruises easily, thin skin, sleeps badly, feels “puffy” and a bit irritable. No fractures or falls.
No steroid emergency card. Did not know she shouldn’t stop suddenly. Had flu and pneumonia vaccines last year; no shingles vaccine.
Widowed. Collects her grandchildren from school three days a week. “If I can’t do that, my daughter can’t work.”

Determined about 15 mg. A bit sheepish when asked how she is actually taking the tablets. Accepts a plan if her symptoms are taken seriously, she understands the harms of high doses, and she is referred to a specialist.

ice.ideas: “The higher dose is the only thing that works, so I should stay on it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: she has already self-increased to 15 mg and stopped her bone tablets, and feels guilty; frightened of becoming disabled and unable to help her daughter with the grandchildren.

cues: Relapse each time below 7.5 mg — the dose at which she was last well matters.
“That worked” — she may already be taking it; ask exactly how she takes her tablets.

checkpoints.text: Confirms the pattern of PMR relapse (girdle pain and stiffness returning as the dose falls) and interprets the raised CRP and ESR in that context

Screens for giant cell arteritis (headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms) and for alternative diagnoses (peripheral synovitis suggesting rheumatoid arthritis, infection, malignancy, weight loss)
Asks exactly how she is taking the medicines and identifies the self-increase to 15 mg and the stopped alendronate

Agrees a safe dose plan in line with BSR 2024: return to the dose at which she was last symptom-free rather than 15 mg, step down from her current dose without stopping abruptly, then taper more slowly (check the SPC/local formulary)
Reviews steroid harms: confirms the raised HbA1c and BP and plans follow-up, discusses weight, skin, sleep and mood

Addresses bone health: explains why bone protection matters on long-term glucocorticoids, manages the heartburn and restarts or changes treatment (for example taking alendronate correctly, or an alternative), with DXA as appropriate
Issues an NHS steroid emergency card and explains sick-day rules and never stopping suddenly; offers shingles vaccination as appropriate
Refers to rheumatology for relapsing PMR and consideration of steroid-sparing treatment, and safety-nets for GCA symptoms (same-day) and adrenal crisis

worked.txt: “Lots of people adjust their tablets when they feel bad. Can you tell me exactly how you’ve been taking them this last week or two?”
“Any new headache, tenderness on your scalp when you brush your hair, pain in your jaw when you chew, or any change in your eyesight?”

“15 mg worked, but it was the dose to switch the illness off. The guidance is to go back to the dose where you were last well, around 10, then come down more slowly. That controls it with fewer side effects.”
“The steroids are pushing your sugar and blood pressure up and thinning your skin and bones. That’s why we want the lowest dose that controls it, and why the bone tablets matter.”
“Because you’ve been on steroids a long time, your body relies on them. Never stop them suddenly, and carry this steroid card so anyone treating you in an emergency knows.”
“When PMR keeps coming back as we reduce the steroid, the guidance is to involve the rheumatologists. There are other medicines that can help you need less steroid.”

f.learning: Relapse during glucocorticoid tapering is common in polymyalgia rheumatica. A relapse is the return of PMR symptoms, usually with rising inflammatory markers; raised markers alone without symptoms are not a relapse. The BSR 2024 guideline advises, for a relapse, returning to the previous dose at which the person was well (rather than restarting the initial dose), then tapering more slowly, and referring to specialist care for relapsing disease, inability to taper, or prolonged steroid need, where steroid-sparing treatment (such as methotrexate, or a biologic in some cases) can be considered. Every relapse should prompt a GCA screen (new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms need same-day assessment) and reconsideration of alternative diagnoses (late-onset rheumatoid arthritis, infection, malignancy). Ask exactly how the person is taking their tablets: self-adjustment is common. Long-term glucocorticoids cause weight gain, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, skin thinning, sleep and mood disturbance, cataract and osteoporosis. Bone protection is recommended for most older people expected to take glucocorticoids for 3 months or more (NOGG guidance); if alendronate causes heartburn, check it is taken correctly and consider alternatives, and assess fracture risk. The National Patient Safety Alert on steroid emergency cards (2020) requires people at risk of adrenal insufficiency, including those on prednisolone 5 mg or more for 4 weeks or longer, to be given an NHS steroid emergency card and sick-day advice; steroids must never be stopped abruptly. Offer recommended vaccinations, including shingles vaccination (non-live) for eligible people. The communication task is respecting her lived experience of relapse and her caring role while negotiating a safer dose plan.

model.text: Hello Mrs Doyle, I’m Dr Clarke. How have things been with the PMR?
Every time we cut the steroids, the stiffness comes straight back. I can barely get out of bed. I want to go back to 15 milligrams, that worked, and just stay on it.
That sounds really frustrating. Let’s work out what’s happening and get you a plan that holds. When does the stiffness come back?
Every time it goes under seven and a half. Within a fortnight my shoulders and hips are back to how they were at the start.
Any new headache, tenderness on your scalp when you brush your hair, pain in your jaw when you chew, or any change in your eyesight?
No, none of that.
Any swollen joints in your hands or feet, fevers, sweats or weight loss you can’t explain?
No. I’ve put weight on, if anything. Six kilos.
Lots of people adjust their tablets when they feel bad. Can you tell me exactly how you’ve been taking them this last week or two?
(pause) I went back to 15 ten days ago. I had an old box. And I stopped the bone tablet a few months ago, it gave me heartburn.
Thank you for telling me, that really helps. Has the 15 helped?
Much better. But I’m puffy, I bruise, I can’t sleep.
What worries you most about the PMR?
Becoming disabled. I collect the grandchildren three days a week. If I can’t, my daughter can’t work.

Your bloods show the inflammation has come back, which fits the stiffness. That’s called a relapse, and it’s common. The guidance is not to go back to the starting dose but to the dose where you were last well, around 10, and then come down much more slowly. That controls it with fewer side effects.
But 15 works.

It does, and it’s also pushing your sugar and blood pressure up, and thinning your skin and bones. Staying on 15 long term would cause more harm than help. Since you’re on 15 now, we’ll step down to 10 rather than stopping suddenly, and I’ll write it down for you.
model.why: Harms; safe step-down from current dose

model.text: Because the PMR keeps returning as we reduce, I’m going to refer you to the rheumatologists. There are other medicines that can help you need less steroid.

For your bones: the steroids make them thinner, so protection really matters. The heartburn might settle if the tablet is taken first thing with a full glass of water, standing up for 30 minutes. If not, there are other options, and I’d like to check your bone density.

One important safety thing: after this long on steroids, your body relies on them. Never stop them suddenly, and carry this steroid emergency card. If you’re vomiting and can’t keep them down, you need medical help the same day.
Your sugar has crept up to just below the diabetes range, so I’ll repeat it and recheck your blood pressure. And you’re eligible for the shingles vaccine, which I’d recommend.
Can you tell me the plan?
Down to 10, not stopping suddenly. Come down slower later. Rheumatology. Bone tablet properly or something else, and a scan. Carry the card. Sugar test, blood pressure, shingles jab.
Perfect. If you get a new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when eating, or any change in your eyesight, that’s same-day, call us or 111. I’ll see you in four weeks.
